title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 5
paragraphs: "And what do you make of this latest farce — the coronation in Milan?" asked Anna Pavlovna. "And the comedy of the people of Genoa and Lucca presenting their petitions to Monsieur Bonaparte, while Monsieur Bonaparte sits on a throne and graciously grants the wishes of nations? It's beyond belief! It's enough to make your head spin! It's as if the whole world has gone mad."
Prince Andrei looked Anna Pavlovna straight in the face with a sardonic smile.
[Speaking in French] "'God has given it to me — let anyone who touches it beware!'" he said, then repeated the words in Italian: [Speaking in Italian] "'Dio mi l'ha dato. Guai a chi la tocchi!'"
* God has given it to me, let him who touches it beware!
"I hope this will be the last straw," Anna Pavlovna continued. "The sovereigns will not be able to tolerate this man who threatens everything."

[Speaking in French] "The sovereigns? I'm not speaking of Russia," said the vicomte, politely but without hope. "The sovereigns, madame — what have they done for Louis XVII, for the Queen, for Madame Elizabeth? Nothing!" He grew more animated. "And believe me, they are reaping what they sowed when they betrayed the Bourbon cause. The sovereigns! They're sending ambassadors to congratulate the usurper."
He sighed disdainfully and shifted his position again.

Prince Hippolyte, who had been staring at the vicomte through his eyeglass for some time, suddenly turned his whole body toward the little princess and, asking her for a needle, began tracing the Condé coat of arms on the table. He explained it to her with as much gravity as if she had asked him to do it.
[Speaking in French] "A red baton, engrailed, on an azure field — the house of Condé," he said.
The princess listened with a smile.

"If Bonaparte remains on the throne of France for another year," the vicomte continued, with the air of a man who, being better informed than anyone else on the subject, doesn't listen to others but follows his own train of thought, "things will have gone too far. Through intrigue, violence, exile, and executions, French society — I mean good French society — will have been destroyed forever, and then..."
He shrugged his shoulders and spread his hands. Pierre wanted to say something — the conversation interested him — but Anna Pavlovna, who had been watching him, cut in first.

"Emperor Alexander," she said, with the melancholy that always accompanied any mention she made of the imperial family, "has declared that he will leave it to the French people to choose their own form of government. And I believe that once they are free of the usurper, the entire nation will throw itself into the arms of its rightful king," she concluded, trying to be gracious toward the royalist émigré.
"That's doubtful," said Prince Andrei. "The vicomte is quite right in saying that things have already gone too far. I think it will be very difficult to go back to the old order."
"From what I've heard," said Pierre, blushing as he broke into the conversation, "almost the entire aristocracy has already gone over to Bonaparte's side."
"That's what the Bonapartists say," replied the vicomte, without looking at Pierre. "At the present time it's hard to know the true state of French public opinion."
"Bonaparte himself has said so," remarked Prince Andrei with a sarcastic smile.
It was clear that he didn't like the vicomte and was directing his remarks at him, even while avoiding his gaze.

"'I showed them the path to glory, but they did not follow it,'" Prince Andrei continued after a brief silence, again quoting Napoleon's words. "'I opened my antechambers and they came crowding in.' I don't know how far he was justified in saying that."

"Not in the least," replied the vicomte. "After the murder of the duc, even his most devoted admirers stopped calling him a hero. If to some people," he went on, turning to Anna Pavlovna, "he ever was a hero, after the murder of the duc there was one more martyr in heaven and one fewer hero on earth."

Before Anna Pavlovna and the others could smile their appreciation of this neat line, Pierre broke into the conversation again, and though Anna Pavlovna was certain he would say something inappropriate, she was unable to stop him.

"The execution of the Duc d'Enghien," declared Pierre, "was a political necessity, and it seems to me that Napoleon showed greatness of soul by taking the full responsibility for that act upon himself."
[Speaking in French] "God! My God!" murmured Anna Pavlovna in a horrified whisper.
"What, Monsieur Pierre — you think assassination shows greatness of soul?" said the little princess, smiling and pulling her embroidery closer.
"Oh! Oh!" exclaimed several voices.
"Capital!" said Prince Hippolyte in English, and began slapping his knee with his palm.
The vicomte merely shrugged his shoulders. Pierre looked solemnly at his audience over his spectacles and continued.

"I say this," he went on with growing intensity, "because the Bourbons fled from the Revolution and abandoned the people to chaos. Napoleon alone understood the Revolution and brought it under control, and so, for the general good, he could not stop short on account of one man's life."
"Won't you come over to the other table?" suggested Anna Pavlovna.
But Pierre went on without paying her any attention.

"No," he cried, growing more and more passionate, "Napoleon is great because he rose above the Revolution, stamped out its worst excesses, and preserved everything good in it — equality before the law, freedom of speech, freedom of the press — and that is the only reason he gained power."
"Yes — if, having gained power, he had restored it to the rightful king instead of using it to commit murder, then I would call him a great man," remarked the vicomte.

"He couldn't do that. The people gave him power so that he could rid them of the Bourbons, and because they recognized that he was a great man. The Revolution was a magnificent thing!" declared Pierre, betraying by this reckless and provocative statement his extreme youth and his eagerness to say everything that was on his mind.
"What? Revolution and regicide — a magnificent thing? Well, after that... But won't you come to the other table?" Anna Pavlovna repeated.
[Speaking in French] "Rousseau's Social Contract," said the vicomte with a condescending smile.
"I'm not talking about regicide. I'm talking about ideas."
"Yes — ideas of robbery, murder, and regicide," someone interjected in an ironic voice.
"Those were extremes, certainly, but they aren't the main point. What matters are the rights of man, the liberation from prejudice, equality before the law — and Napoleon has upheld all of these."

"Liberty and equality," said the vicomte with contempt, as though finally deciding to demonstrate to this young man how foolish his words were. "Grand phrases that have long been discredited. Who doesn't love liberty and equality? Even our Savior preached liberty and equality. Have people become happier since the Revolution? On the contrary. We wanted freedom, and Bonaparte has destroyed it."

Prince Andrei watched with an amused smile, looking from Pierre to the vicomte and from the vicomte to their hostess. In the first moment of Pierre's outburst, Anna Pavlovna had been horrified, despite all her social experience. But when she saw that Pierre's blasphemous words had not outraged the vicomte, and had satisfied herself that it was impossible to shut Pierre up, she rallied her forces and joined the vicomte in a vigorous counterattack on the young orator.

[Speaking in French] "But my dear Monsieur Pierre," she said, "how do you explain the fact that a great man would execute a duke — or even an ordinary person — who is innocent and has not been tried?"
"I would like to ask," said the vicomte, "how monsieur explains the 18th Brumaire. Was that not a fraud? It was a swindle, pure and simple — nothing like the behavior of a great man!"
"And the prisoners he killed in Africa! That was horrible!" said the little princess, shrugging her shoulders.
"He's a despicable man, no matter what anyone says," remarked Prince Hippolyte.

Pierre, not knowing whom to answer, looked around at all of them and smiled. His smile was unlike the half-smiles of other people. When he smiled, his serious, even somewhat gloomy expression was instantly replaced by something else — a childlike, kind, even slightly foolish look that seemed to ask forgiveness.
The vicomte, who was meeting Pierre for the first time, saw clearly that this young radical was not nearly as dangerous as his words suggested. Everyone fell silent.

"How do you expect him to answer all of you at once?" said Prince Andrei. "Besides, when judging a statesman, you have to distinguish between his actions as a private individual, as a general, and as an emperor. At least that's how it seems to me."
"Yes, yes — exactly!" Pierre chimed in, delighted at this reinforcement.

"One must admit," Prince Andrei continued, "that Napoleon the man was great on the bridge at Arcola, and in the hospital at Jaffa where he clasped the hands of plague victims. But... there are other actions that are hard to justify."
Prince Andrei, who had clearly been trying to soften the awkwardness of Pierre's remarks, stood up and signaled to his wife that it was time to go.
Suddenly Prince Hippolyte jumped up, gestured for everyone's attention, and asked them all to sit down, then began:

"I was told the most charming Moscow story today, and I simply must share it with you. Excuse me, Vicomte — I have to tell it in Russian or the whole point will be lost." And Prince Hippolyte launched into his story in the kind of Russian a Frenchman would speak after about a year in Russia. Everyone waited, so insistently did he demand their attention.

"There is a lady in Moscow — une dame — and she is very stingy. She insists on having two footmen behind her carriage, and very big ones. That's what she likes. And she had a maid, also big. She said..."
Here Prince Hippolyte paused, visibly struggling to recall his thoughts.
"She said... Oh yes! She said, 'Girl' — to the maid — 'put on a livery, get up behind the carriage, and come with me while I make some calls.'"
Here Prince Hippolyte sputtered and burst out laughing long before his audience, which did not help the story. A few people, including the elderly lady and Anna Pavlovna, did manage a smile.

"She went. Suddenly there was a great gust of wind. The girl lost her hat and her long hair came tumbling down..." Here he could barely get the words out through his gasps of laughter: "And the whole world found out..."

And so the story ended. Although it was impossible to say why he had told it, or why it had to be told in Russian, still, Anna Pavlovna and the others appreciated Prince Hippolyte's social instinct in so neatly defusing Pierre's uncomfortable and graceless outburst. After the anecdote, the conversation dissolved into harmless small talk about the latest ball and the next one, about the theater, and about who would see whom, and when and where.

title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 19
paragraphs: At the men's end of the table the conversation grew more and more animated. The colonel told them that the declaration of war had already appeared in Petersburg and that a copy, which he had seen with his own eyes, had been sent that very day by courier to the commander in chief.
"And why the hell are we going to fight Bonaparte?" Shinshin remarked. "He's already shut Austria up, and I'm afraid we're next."
The colonel was a stout, tall, red-faced German, clearly devoted to the military and patriotically Russian. He took offense at Shinshin's comment.

"It is because, my good sir," he said, speaking with a heavy German accent, "because ze Emperor knows zat. He says in ze manifesto zat he cannot look wiz indifference at ze danger zreatening Russia, and zat ze safety and dignity of ze Empire, as well as ze sanctity of its alliances..." He emphasized this last word as if it contained the whole point of the matter.
Then, with the flawless official memory that characterized him, he recited the opening words of the manifesto:

...and the wish, which constitutes the Emperor's sole and absolute aim—to establish peace in Europe on firm foundations—has now decided him to dispatch part of the army abroad and to create a new condition for the attainment of that purpose.
"Zat, my dear sir, is vy..." he concluded, drinking a glass of wine with dignity and looking to the count for approval.

[Speaking in French] "Do you know the proverb: 'Jerome, Jerome, don't roam—stay home and turn your spindles'?" said Shinshin, wrinkling his brow and smiling. [Speaking in French] "That suits us perfectly. Suvorov, now—he knew what he was doing, and even he was beaten to a pulp. And where are we going to find a Suvorov today? [Speaking in French] I ask you." He kept switching between French and Russian.
* Do you know the proverb?
* (2) That suits us down to the ground.
* (3) Hollow.
* (4) I just ask you that.

"Ve must fight to the last d-d-drop of our blood!" the colonel shouted, thumping the table. "And ve must die for our Emperor, and zen all vill be vell. And ve must discuss it as little as p-p-possible"—he lingered on the word—"as p-p-possible," he repeated, turning once more to the count. "Zat is how ve old hussars see it, and zere's an end of it! And how do you, a young man and a young hussar—how do you see it?" he added, turning to Nicholas, who had swiveled away from his dinner partner the moment he heard the war being discussed, all eyes and ears on the colonel.

"I completely agree with you," Nicholas replied, flaring up. He turned his plate around and shifted his wineglasses about with the same decisiveness and desperation as if he were facing mortal danger at that very moment. "I am convinced that we Russians must die or conquer," he concluded—aware, as was everyone else, that his words had come out too passionate and dramatic for the occasion and were therefore awkward.
"What you just said was splendid!" said his dinner partner Julie.
Sonya trembled from head to toe and blushed to her ears, behind her ears, and all the way down her neck and shoulders while Nicholas was speaking.
Pierre had been listening to the colonel's speech and nodding in agreement.
"That's fine," he said.
"The young man's a true hussar!" shouted the colonel, thumping the table again.

"What's all that racket down there?" Marya Dmitrievna's deep voice suddenly demanded from the other end of the table. "What are you banging the table for?" she said to the hussar. "And why are you getting so worked up? Do you think the French are here?"
"I am speaking ze truce," the hussar replied with a smile.
"It's all about the war," the count called down the table. "You know my son is going, Marya Dmitrievna? My son is going."

"I have four sons in the army, but I don't sit here worrying. It's all in God's hands. You can die in your bed, or God may spare you on the battlefield," Marya Dmitrievna replied in her deep voice, which carried easily the full length of the table.
"That's true!"
Once again the conversation split in two—the ladies' at one end, the men's at the other.
"You won't ask," Natasha's little brother was saying. "I know you won't ask!"
"I will," replied Natasha.
Her face suddenly flushed with reckless, joyous determination. She half rose, caught Pierre's eye across the table to make sure he was watching what was coming, and turned to her mother.
"Mama!" rang out the clear contralto of her childish voice, audible the whole length of the table.
"What is it?" asked the countess, startled. But seeing from her daughter's face that it was only mischief, she wagged a stern, threatening finger at her.
The conversation died down.
"Mama! What sweets are we going to have?" Natasha's voice sounded even firmer and more resolute now.
The countess tried to frown but couldn't manage it. Marya Dmitrievna shook her thick finger.
"Cossack!" she said threateningly.
Most of the guests, unsure how to react to this outburst, looked at the elders.
"You'd better watch yourself!" said the countess.
"Mama! What sweets are we going to have?" Natasha cried again, boldly, with cheeky delight, confident her prank would be taken in good humor.
Sonya and chubby little Petya doubled over with laughter.
"You see? I asked," Natasha whispered to her little brother and to Pierre, glancing at him again.
"Ice pudding—but you won't get any," said Marya Dmitrievna.
Natasha saw there was nothing to be afraid of and decided to take on even Marya Dmitrievna.
"Marya Dmitrievna! What kind of ice pudding? I don't like ice cream."
"Carrot ices."
"No! What kind, Marya Dmitrievna? What kind?" she practically screamed. "I want to know!"

Marya Dmitrievna and the countess burst out laughing, and all the guests joined in. Everyone laughed not at Marya Dmitrievna's answer but at the unbelievable boldness and spunk of this little girl who had dared to challenge Marya Dmitrievna like that.

Natasha only gave up when she'd been told there would be pineapple ice cream. Before the ices, champagne was served. The band struck up again, the count and countess kissed, and the guests rose from their seats to "congratulate" the countess, reaching across the table to clink glasses with the count, the children, and one another. Once more the footmen rushed about, chairs scraped, and in the same order as they had entered—but with redder faces—the guests filed back into the drawing room and the count's study.

title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 22
paragraphs: While these conversations were taking place in the reception room and the princess's room, a carriage carrying Pierre—who had been sent for—and Anna Mikhaylovna, who felt it necessary to accompany him, was pulling into the courtyard of Count Bezukhov's house. As the wheels rolled softly over the straw that had been laid beneath the windows, Anna Mikhaylovna turned to offer some comforting words to her companion—and realized he was asleep in his corner. She woke him up. Pierre roused himself and followed Anna Mikhaylovna out of the carriage, only then beginning to think about the visit with his dying father that lay ahead. He noticed they hadn't come to the front entrance but to a back door. As he was climbing down from the carriage, two men who looked like tradesmen darted away from the entrance and hid in the shadows along the wall. Pausing, Pierre spotted several other men of the same type lurking in the shadows on both sides of the house. But neither Anna Mikhaylovna nor the footman nor the coachman—who couldn't have missed seeing them—paid any attention. "It must be all right," Pierre told himself, and followed Anna Mikhaylovna. She hurried up a narrow, dimly lit stone staircase, calling back to Pierre, who was falling behind, to keep up. Though he couldn't see why it was necessary for him to visit the count at all, much less why they had to use the back stairs, Anna Mikhaylovna's air of confidence and urgency made Pierre conclude that it was all absolutely essential. Halfway up, they were nearly knocked over by some men carrying pails who came clattering down the stairs in heavy boots. These men pressed themselves against the wall to let Pierre and Anna Mikhaylovna pass, showing not the slightest surprise at seeing them there.
"Is this the way to the princesses' apartments?" Anna Mikhaylovna asked one of them.
"Yes," a footman answered in a bold, loud voice, as though anything were now permissible. "The door on the left, ma'am."
"Perhaps the count didn't ask for me," Pierre said when they reached the landing. "I'd better go to my own room."
Anna Mikhaylovna stopped and waited for him to catch up.
"Oh, my friend!" she said, touching his arm just as she had touched her son's that afternoon. "Believe me, I'm suffering no less than you are, but be a man!"
"But really, shouldn't I just go?" he asked, looking at her kindly over his spectacles.

"Oh, my dear friend! Forget whatever wrongs may have been done to you. Remember—he is your father... perhaps in the agony of death." She sighed. "I've loved you like a son from the very beginning. Trust me, Pierre. I won't forget your interests."
Pierre didn't understand a word of this, but his growing conviction that all of it was necessary only strengthened, and he meekly followed Anna Mikhaylovna, who was already opening a door.

The door led into a back anteroom. In one corner, an old servant of the princesses sat knitting a stocking. Pierre had never been in this part of the house and didn't even know these rooms existed. Anna Mikhaylovna addressed a maid hurrying past with a decanter on a tray as "my dear" and "my sweet," asked about the princess's health, and then led Pierre down a stone passage. The first door on the left opened into the princesses' apartments. The maid with the decanter, in her haste, had left the door open—everything in the house was being done in haste just then—and as Pierre and Anna Mikhaylovna passed, they instinctively glanced inside. There sat Prince Vasili and the eldest princess, close together, talking intensely. Seeing them pass, Prince Vasili drew back with obvious irritation, while the princess leaped up and, in a gesture of desperation, slammed the door shut with all her strength.

This was so unlike the princess's usual composure, and the fear on Prince Vasili's face so out of keeping with his dignity, that Pierre stopped and looked questioningly over his spectacles at his guide. Anna Mikhaylovna showed no surprise. She only gave a faint smile and sighed, as if to say this was no more than she had expected.
"Be a man, my friend. I'll look after your interests," she said in response to his look, and walked even faster down the corridor.

Pierre couldn't make sense of any of it, least of all what "looking after his interests" meant, but he decided that all these things simply had to happen. From the corridor they entered a large, dimly lit room next to the count's reception room. It was one of those grand but cold apartments Pierre knew only from approaching through the front entrance, but now even this room had an empty bathtub standing in it, and water had been spilled on the carpet. A deacon with a censer and a servant passed them on tiptoe without so much as a glance. They continued into the reception room that Pierre knew well, with its two Italian windows facing the conservatory, its large bust, and its full-length portrait of Catherine the Great. The same people sat there in nearly the same positions as before, whispering among themselves. They all fell silent and turned to look at Anna Mikhaylovna—pale and tear-stained—as she entered, and at Pierre's large, heavy figure following meekly behind her with his head bowed.

Anna Mikhaylovna's expression conveyed her awareness that the decisive moment had arrived. With the manner of a practical Petersburg lady, she entered the room even more boldly than she had that afternoon, keeping Pierre close beside her. She knew that by bringing the person the dying man had asked to see, her own presence was assured. Scanning the room with a quick glance and noticing the count's confessor, she glided over to him in a kind of half-bow—seeming to grow suddenly smaller—and respectfully received the blessing first of one priest, then another.
"Thank God you've come in time," she said to one of the priests. "We relatives have all been so worried. This young man is the count's son," she added more softly. "What a terrible moment!"
Then she went up to the doctor.
"Dear doctor," she said, "this young man is the count's son. Is there any hope?"

The doctor glanced upward quickly and gave a silent shrug. Anna Mikhaylovna mirrored the exact same movement—raising her shoulders and eyes, nearly closing them—sighed, and turned away from the doctor to Pierre. In a particularly respectful and tenderly sorrowful voice, she said:
"Trust in His mercy!" Then, pointing him to a small sofa where he could sit and wait, she moved silently toward the door everyone was watching. It gave a faint creak as she disappeared behind it.

Pierre, having resolved to obey his guide in everything, moved toward the sofa she had indicated. The moment Anna Mikhaylovna vanished, he noticed that every pair of eyes in the room was fixed on him with something more than curiosity and sympathy. People whispered to one another, casting meaningful glances his way with a kind of awe—even deference. He had never been treated like this before. A strange lady, the one who had been talking with the priests, stood up and offered him her seat. An aide-de-camp picked up a glove Pierre had dropped and returned it to him. The doctors fell respectfully silent as he passed and moved aside for him. At first Pierre wanted to take a different seat so as not to inconvenience the lady, and to pick up the glove himself, and to walk around the doctors who weren't even in his way. But all at once he sensed that this wouldn't do—that tonight he was a person expected to perform some kind of solemn ritual, and therefore obliged to accept their attentions. He took the glove from the aide-de-camp in silence, sat down in the lady's chair, and placed his large hands symmetrically on his knees in the naive pose of an Egyptian statue. He had decided that in order not to lose his head and do something foolish, he must not act on his own judgment tonight but surrender himself entirely to the will of those guiding him.

Less than two minutes later, Prince Vasili entered the room with his head held high, looking majestic. He wore his long coat with three stars on his chest. He seemed even thinner than he had that morning; his eyes appeared larger than usual as he surveyed the room and spotted Pierre. He walked over, took Pierre's hand—something he had never done before—and pulled it downward, as if testing whether it was firmly attached.
"Courage, courage, my friend! He's asked to see you. That's good!" And he turned to go.
But Pierre felt he should ask: "How is..." He hesitated, unsure whether it was proper to call the dying man "the count," yet embarrassed to call him "father."
"He had another stroke about half an hour ago. Courage, my friend..."

Pierre's mind was in such a fog that the word "stroke" made him think of a physical blow. He stared at Prince Vasili in confusion, and only later grasped that a stroke meant an attack of illness. Prince Vasili murmured something to Lorrain in passing and went through the door on tiptoe. He wasn't good at walking on tiptoe, and his whole body lurched with each step. The eldest princess followed him, and the priests, deacons, and some servants also went through the door. Behind it came the sound of things being moved around, and finally Anna Mikhaylovna—still wearing the same expression, pale but resolute in the performance of duty—hurried out, lightly touched Pierre's arm, and said:
"God's mercy is boundless! They are about to administer last rites. Come."

Pierre went through the door, stepping onto the soft carpet, and noticed that the strange lady, the aide-de-camp, and several servants all followed him in, as though there were no longer any need for permission to enter that room.

title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter 3
paragraphs: Returning from the review, Kutuzov brought the Austrian general to his private room and, calling for his adjutant, asked for papers on the condition of the arriving troops and the letters that had come from Archduke Ferdinand, who commanded the advance army. Prince Andrew Bolkonsky entered the room with the requested documents. Kutuzov and the Austrian member of the Hofkriegsrath were sitting at a table with a map spread out before them.
[speaking in French] "Ah..." said Kutuzov, glancing at Bolkonsky as though asking the adjutant to wait, and went on speaking in French.

[speaking in French] "All I can say, General," he began with an elegant pleasantness of tone and delivery that made you want to listen to each carefully chosen word — it was clear Kutuzov enjoyed the sound of his own voice — "all I can say, General, is that if the matter depended solely on my personal wishes, His Majesty Emperor Francis's will would have been fulfilled long ago. I would have joined the Archduke without delay. And believe me, on my honor, it would be a genuine pleasure for me to hand over supreme command of the army to a more knowledgeable and capable general — of whom Austria has so many — and to lay down this heavy burden of responsibility. But circumstances are sometimes stronger than we are, General."

Kutuzov smiled in a way that seemed to say: You're perfectly free not to believe me, and I really don't care whether you do or not — but you have no grounds for calling me a liar. And that's the whole point.
The Austrian general looked displeased but had no choice except to respond in the same tone.

"On the contrary," he said in a querulous, irritated voice that clashed with his flattering words, "on the contrary — Your Excellency's participation in the joint effort is highly valued by His Majesty. But we believe this current delay is robbing the splendid Russian troops and their commander of the laurels they have so often won in battle." He finished what was clearly a rehearsed speech.
Kutuzov bowed, wearing the same smile.

"But that is my conviction, and judging by the most recent letter with which His Highness Archduke Ferdinand has honored me, I would assume the Austrian forces, under the direction of so skilled a commander as General Mack, have already won a decisive victory and no longer require our assistance," said Kutuzov.

The general frowned. Although there was no confirmed news of an Austrian defeat, too many troubling rumors were circulating for comfort, and Kutuzov's cheerful mention of an Austrian victory sounded suspiciously like sarcasm. But Kutuzov went on smiling blandly with the same expression — as if he had every right to think so. And in fact, the most recent dispatch from Mack's army had reported a victory and described the army's strategic position as highly favorable.

"Let me see that letter," said Kutuzov, turning to Prince Andrew. "Have a look at this" — and with an ironic smile playing at the corners of his mouth, Kutuzov read aloud to the Austrian general the following passage, in German, from Archduke Ferdinand's letter:

We have fully concentrated forces of nearly seventy thousand men with which to attack and defeat the enemy should he cross the Lech. Also, as we command Ulm, we cannot be deprived of the advantage of holding both sides of the Danube, so that should the enemy not cross the Lech, we can cross the Danube, throw ourselves on his line of communications, recross the river further downstream, and frustrate his intentions should he try to direct his whole force against our faithful ally. We shall therefore confidently await the moment when the Imperial Russian army is fully equipped, and shall then, in conjunction with it, easily find a way to deliver the enemy the fate he deserves.
Kutuzov sighed deeply when he finished reading and looked at the Hofkriegsrath member with a mild, attentive gaze.

[speaking in French] "But you know the wise maxim, Your Excellency — always prepare for the worst," said the Austrian general, clearly wanting to move past the sarcasm and get down to business. He glanced involuntarily at the aide-de-camp.

[speaking in French] "Excuse me, General," Kutuzov interrupted, also turning to Prince Andrew. "Here's what I need, my dear fellow: get all the scout reports from Kozlovsky. Here are two letters from Count Nostitz, and here's one from His Highness Archduke Ferdinand, plus these" — he handed over several papers — "put together a clean memo in French summarizing everything we know about the Austrian army's movements, then deliver it to His Excellency."

Prince Andrew nodded to show he had understood from the first word — not only what was said, but what Kutuzov actually meant behind it. He gathered the papers and, with a bow to both men, stepped quietly across the carpet and into the anteroom.

Although not much time had passed since Prince Andrew left Russia, the change in him was remarkable. In the expression on his face, in his gestures, in the way he walked, almost no trace remained of his former mannered laziness and indifference. He now looked like a man who has no time to think about the impression he makes on others because he is absorbed in meaningful, engaging work. His face showed more contentment with himself and those around him; his smile and his eyes were brighter, more appealing.

Kutuzov, whom he had caught up with in Poland, had received him warmly, promised not to forget him, singled him out from the other adjutants, and brought him along to Vienna, entrusting him with the more important assignments. From Vienna, Kutuzov had written to his old comrade, Prince Andrew's father:
Your son gives every promise of becoming an officer distinguished by his diligence, resolve, and competence. I consider myself fortunate to have such a subordinate at my side.

On Kutuzov's staff, among his fellow officers and in the army at large, Prince Andrew had — just as in Petersburg society — two sharply opposite reputations. A minority recognized him as someone different from themselves and everyone else, expected great things of him, listened to him, admired and imitated him. With these people, Prince Andrew was natural and at ease. The majority, however, disliked him and thought him arrogant, cold, and unpleasant. But among this group, Prince Andrew knew how to carry himself in a way that commanded their respect and even their fear.
Coming out of Kutuzov's room with the papers in hand, Prince Andrew walked up to his comrade Kozlovsky, the aide-de-camp on duty, who was sitting by the window reading a book.
"Well, Prince?" Kozlovsky asked.
"I've been ordered to write a memo explaining why we aren't advancing."
"And why aren't we?"
Prince Andrew shrugged.
"Any news from Mack?"
"No."
"If he'd really been defeated, we'd have heard by now."
"Probably," said Prince Andrew, and started toward the outer door.

But at that instant, a tall Austrian general in a greatcoat strode in quickly, slamming the door behind him. He wore the Order of Maria Theresa around his neck and had a black bandage wrapped around his head. He had obviously just arrived.
"Commander in Chief Kutuzov?" the newcomer demanded, speaking quickly in a harsh German accent, looking both ways and heading straight for the inner door.
"The commander in chief is in a meeting," said Kozlovsky, hurrying up to block his path. "Whom shall I announce?"
The unknown general looked down at the rather short Kozlovsky with contempt, as if astonished that anyone could fail to recognize him.
"The commander in chief is in a meeting," Kozlovsky repeated calmly.

The general's face darkened. His lips trembled. He pulled out a notebook, scribbled something in pencil, tore out the page, thrust it at Kozlovsky, then strode to the window and threw himself into a chair, glaring around the room as if to ask: Why are they all staring at me? He raised his head and stretched his neck as though about to speak, but then, with forced indifference, began humming to himself — and the odd sound broke off almost immediately. The door to the private room opened and Kutuzov appeared in the doorway. The general with the bandaged head jerked forward as if fleeing some danger and, taking long, rapid strides on his thin legs, rushed up to Kutuzov.
[speaking in French] "You see before you the unfortunate Mack," he said in a broken voice.

Kutuzov's face, framed in the open doorway, remained completely still for several seconds. Then a wave of wrinkles passed across it, his forehead smoothed again, and he bowed his head respectfully, closed his eyes, silently let Mack walk past him into the room, and shut the door behind them both.

The rumor that the Austrians had been crushed and that the entire army had surrendered at Ulm turned out to be true. Within half an hour, adjutants were being dispatched in every direction with orders that made it clear the Russian army, inactive until now, would soon have to face the enemy.

Prince Andrew was one of those rare staff officers whose deepest interest lay in the overall course of the war. When he saw Mack and heard the details of the catastrophe, he immediately grasped that half the campaign was already lost. He vividly understood the full difficulty of the Russian army's position and could picture exactly what lay ahead and what role he would have to play. In spite of himself, he felt a surge of excitement at the thought of arrogant Austria's humiliation, and at the prospect that within a week he might witness — and take part in — the first clash between Russian and French forces since the days of Suvorov. He feared that Napoleon's genius might overwhelm Russian courage, yet at the same time he could not bear the thought of his hero being disgraced.

Agitated and unsettled by these thoughts, Prince Andrew headed to his room to write to his father, as he did every day. In the corridor he ran into Nesvitsky, with whom he shared quarters, and the joker Zherkov. As usual, they were laughing.
"Why so grim?" Nesvitsky asked, noticing Prince Andrew's pale face and glittering eyes.
"There's nothing to be cheerful about," Bolkonsky answered.

Just as Prince Andrew encountered Nesvitsky and Zherkov, two men approached from the other end of the corridor: Strauch, an Austrian general on Kutuzov's staff who oversaw provisioning for the Russian army, and the Hofkriegsrath member who had arrived the previous evening. The corridor was wide enough for the generals to pass the three officers without any difficulty, but Zherkov shoved Nesvitsky aside and said in a breathless voice:
"They're coming! They're coming! Step aside — make way, please, make way!"
The generals walked past, clearly trying to avoid any awkward attention. On Zherkov's face there suddenly appeared a stupid grin of delight that he seemed unable to suppress.
[speaking in German] "Your Excellency," he said, stepping forward and addressing the Austrian general, "I have the honor of congratulating you."
He bowed and began scraping first one foot and then the other, clumsy as a child at a dance lesson.
The Hofkriegsrath member eyed him severely, but the earnest stupidity of that beaming smile made it impossible to ignore entirely. He narrowed his eyes to show he was listening.
"I have the honor of congratulating you. General Mack has arrived — perfectly well, just a little bruised right here," Zherkov said, pointing to his own head with a radiant smile.
The general scowled, turned away, and walked on.
[speaking in German] "God, how childish!" he muttered angrily after a few steps.
"Good God, what simplicity!"

Nesvitsky threw his arms around Prince Andrew with a laugh, but Bolkonsky — turning even paler — shoved him away with a furious look and rounded on Zherkov. The anxious irritation triggered by Mack's appearance, the news of his defeat, and the thought of what awaited the Russian army all found an outlet in rage at Zherkov's ill-timed joke.

"If you choose to make a buffoon of yourself, sir," he said sharply, his lower jaw trembling slightly, "I can't stop you. But I warn you: if you dare to play the fool in my presence, I will teach you how to behave."
Nesvitsky and Zherkov were so stunned by this outburst that they stared at Bolkonsky in silent, wide-eyed shock.
"What's the matter? I was only congratulating them," Zherkov said.
"I am not joking with you — be quiet!" Bolkonsky snapped, and taking Nesvitsky by the arm, he walked away from Zherkov, who stood there not knowing what to say.
"Come on, what's gotten into you?" Nesvitsky said, trying to calm him.

"What's gotten into me?" Prince Andrew burst out, stopping in his tracks, his voice shaking with emotion. "Don't you understand? Either we are officers serving our Tsar and our country, who share in its victories and grieve at its misfortunes — or we are nothing but servants who couldn't care less about their master's business. [speaking in French] Forty thousand men slaughtered and the army of our allies destroyed, and you find that amusing! [speaking in French] That's fine for some worthless nobody like that creature you've made your friend, but not for you — not for you. Only a juvenile could find entertainment in this," he added in Russian, though he used the French-accented word for juvenile, noticing that Zherkov could still hear him.
"Forty thousand men massacred and the army of our allies destroyed, and you find that a cause for jesting!"
"It is all very well for that good-for-nothing fellow of whom you have made a friend, but not for you, not for you."
He waited a moment to see if the cornet would respond, but Zherkov turned and walked out of the corridor.

title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 2
paragraphs: In November 1805, Prince Vasili had to make an inspection tour of four different provinces. He had arranged this for himself so he could visit his neglected estates at the same time, pick up his son Anatole from his regiment, and take him to visit old Prince Bolkonsky to arrange a match with the rich old man's daughter. But before leaving home for these new tasks, Prince Vasili had to settle things with Pierre, who had lately been spending whole days at home—that is, at Prince Vasili's house where he was staying—and had been absurd, excited, and foolish in Hélène's presence (as a man in love should be), but had not yet proposed.

"This is all very well, but it needs to be settled," Prince Vasili said to himself with a sorrowful sigh one morning, feeling that Pierre—who was so deeply indebted to him (but never mind that)—was not handling this situation properly. "Youth, foolishness... well, God be with him," he thought, savoring his own generosity, "but it has to come to a head. The day after tomorrow is Lelya's name day. I'll invite two or three people, and if he still doesn't understand what he's supposed to do, then it becomes my responsibility—yes, my responsibility. I am her father."

Six weeks after Anna Pavlovna's party, and after the sleepless night when Pierre had decided that marrying Hélène would be a disaster and he should avoid her and leave, Pierre—despite that decision—had not left Prince Vasili's house. He felt with horror that in everyone's eyes he was being drawn closer to her every day, that he could no longer see her the way he used to, that he couldn't break away from her, and that although it would be terrible, he would have to tie his fate to hers. He might have been able to free himself, but Prince Vasili—who had rarely hosted gatherings before—now threw a party almost every evening at which Pierre had to be present unless he wanted to spoil everyone's enjoyment and disappoint their expectations. In the rare moments when he was home, Prince Vasili would take Pierre's hand in passing and draw it downward, or absent-mindedly offer his wrinkled, clean-shaven cheek for Pierre to kiss, saying: 'See you tomorrow,' or 'Come to dinner or I won't see you,' or 'I'm staying in just for your sake.' And although Prince Vasili, when he stayed in 'for Pierre's sake,' barely exchanged two words with him, Pierre felt he couldn't let him down. Every day he told himself the same thing: 'It's time I figured out who she really is. Was I wrong before, or am I wrong now? No, she's not stupid, she's a wonderful woman,' he sometimes told himself. 'She never makes a mistake, never says anything foolish. She says little, but what she says is always clear and simple—so she can't be stupid. She was never embarrassed and isn't embarrassed now, so she can't be a bad person!' He had often started thinking aloud or making reflections in her company, and she always responded either with a brief, appropriate remark—showing it didn't interest her—or with a silent look and smile that more clearly than anything demonstrated her superiority. She was right to consider all arguments meaningless compared to that smile.

She always greeted him with a radiantly trusting smile meant just for him, a smile with something more significant in it than the general smile that usually brightened her face. Pierre knew that everyone was waiting for him to say a certain word and cross a certain line, and he knew that sooner or later he would cross it. But an incomprehensible terror seized him at the thought of that dreadful step. A thousand times during that month and a half, feeling himself drawn closer and closer to the terrible precipice, Pierre said to himself: 'What am I doing? I need willpower. Don't I have any?'

He wanted to make a decision, but realized with dismay that in this particular matter he lacked the strength of will that he knew he possessed and had demonstrated before. Pierre was one of those people who are strong only when they feel completely innocent, and ever since that day at Anna Pavlovna's when he was overcome with desire while leaning over the snuffbox, an unacknowledged sense of guilt about that desire had paralyzed his will.

On Hélène's name day, a small gathering of 'just family'—as his wife put it—assembled for supper at Prince Vasili's. All these friends and relatives had been given to understand that the young woman's fate would be decided that evening. The guests took their seats at supper. Princess Kuragina, a stout, imposing woman who had once been beautiful, sat at the head of the table. On either side of her were the most important guests—an old general and his wife, and Anna Pavlovna Scherer. At the other end sat the younger and less important guests, along with family members, and there too sat Pierre and Hélène, side by side. Prince Vasili wasn't eating supper; he circled the table in high spirits, sitting down with one guest after another and making casual, pleasant remarks to each—except to Pierre and Hélène, whose presence he seemed not to notice. He kept the whole party lively. The wax candles burned brightly; the silver and crystal gleamed, as did the ladies' gowns and the gold and silver of the men's epaulettes. Servants in scarlet livery moved around the table; the clatter of plates, knives, and glasses blended with the animated buzz of several conversations. At one end, an old chamberlain was assuring an old baroness of his passionate love for her, at which she laughed. At the other end, someone was telling the story of some poor Mary Viktorovna's misfortunes. In the center, Prince Vasili held everyone's attention. With a playful smile, he was telling the ladies about last Wednesday's meeting of the Imperial Council, at which Sergei Kuzmich Vyazminitov, the new military governor general of Petersburg, had received and read the now-famous letter from Emperor Alexander to Sergei Kuzmich. In it, the Emperor said he was receiving declarations of loyalty from all sides, that the one from Petersburg gave him special pleasure, and that he was proud to lead such a nation and would strive to be worthy of it. The letter began: 'Sergei Kuzmich, From all sides reports reach me...' and so on.
"So he never got past 'Sergei Kuzmich'?" asked one of the ladies.

"Exactly—not one word further," answered Prince Vasili, laughing. "'Sergei Kuzmich... From all sides... From all sides... Sergei Kuzmich...' Poor Vyazminitov couldn't get any further! He would start the letter over and over, but every time he said 'Sergei' he would sob, then 'Kuz-mich'—tears—and 'From all sides' would be swallowed up in sobs, and he couldn't go on. And then the handkerchief again, and again: 'Sergei Kuzmich, From all sides...' and more tears, until finally someone else had to read it."
"Kuzmich... From all sides... and then tears," someone repeated, laughing.
"Don't be cruel," cried Anna Pavlovna from her end of the table, wagging her finger. "He is such a fine, worthy man, our dear Vyazminitov..."

Everyone laughed heartily. At the head of the table, where the honored guests sat, everyone seemed to be in high spirits, excited by many things at once. Only Pierre and Hélène sat quietly, almost at the far end, with a suppressed smile on both their faces—a smile that had nothing to do with Sergei Kuzmich, a smile of self-consciousness about their own feelings. But however much the others laughed, talked, joked, and enjoyed their Rhine wine, sauce, and ices, however much they avoided looking at the young couple and seemed oblivious to them, everyone could sense from the occasional glances cast their way that the story about Sergei Kuzmich, the laughter, and the food were all a performance—that the true focus of everyone's attention was Pierre and Hélène. Prince Vasili mimicked Sergei Kuzmich's sobbing while glancing at his daughter, and even as he laughed, his expression clearly said: 'Yes... it's moving along, it will all be settled today.' Anna Pavlovna scolded him on behalf of 'our dear Vyazminitov,' but in her eyes, which briefly met Pierre's, Prince Vasili could read congratulations for his future son-in-law and his daughter's happiness. The old princess sighed sadly as she offered wine to the lady beside her and glanced angrily at her daughter, her sigh seeming to say: 'Yes, there's nothing left for you and me but to sip wine, my dear, now that these young ones are being so bold and shamelessly happy.' 'What nonsense I'm thinking!' thought a diplomat, looking at the lovers' happy faces. 'That's happiness!'

Into this trivial, artificial society had entered the simple power of attraction between a healthy, handsome young man and woman. And this human feeling rose above everything else, towering over all their affected chatter. Jokes fell flat, news failed to interest, and the liveliness was clearly forced. Not just the guests but even the servants waiting at table seemed to sense this, forgetting their duties as they gazed at the beautiful Hélène with her radiant face and at Pierre's broad, red, happy—though uneasy—face. It was as if the very candlelight focused only on those two happy faces.

Pierre felt that he was at the center of it all, which both pleased and embarrassed him. He was like a man completely absorbed in something. He couldn't see, hear, or understand anything clearly. Only now and then, disconnected ideas and impressions from the real world would flash unexpectedly through his mind.

"So it's all settled!" he thought. "But how did it happen? So quickly! Now I know it's not just because of her or just because of me, but because of everyone—it has to happen. They're all expecting it, they're so certain it will happen that I can't, I simply can't, disappoint them. But how will it turn out? I don't know—but it will definitely happen!" thought Pierre, glancing at those dazzling shoulders so close to his eyes.

Or he would suddenly feel ashamed without knowing why. He felt awkward attracting everyone's attention and being considered a lucky man—him, with his plain face, being seen as some kind of Paris who had won a Helen. 'But it always is this way and has to be!' he reassured himself. 'And besides, what did I do to bring it about? How did it start? I came from Moscow with Prince Vasili. Then nothing happened. So why shouldn't I stay at his house? Then I played cards with her and picked up her handbag and went driving with her. How did it start? When did all this happen?' And here he was sitting beside her as her fiancé, seeing, hearing, and feeling her nearness, her breathing, her movements, her beauty. Then it would suddenly seem that it wasn't she who was so beautiful, but he himself, and that's why everyone was looking at him. Flattered by this general admiration, he would puff out his chest, lift his head, and rejoice in his good fortune. Then suddenly a familiar voice repeated something to him for the second time. But Pierre was so lost in thought that he didn't understand.
"I'm asking when you last heard from Bolkonsky," Prince Vasili repeated a third time. "How distracted you are, my dear fellow."

Prince Vasili smiled, and Pierre noticed that everyone was smiling at him and Hélène. 'Well, so what if everyone knows?' thought Pierre. 'So what? It's the truth!' And he gave his gentle, childlike smile, and Hélène smiled too.
"When did the letter arrive? Was it from Olmütz?" repeated Prince Vasili, pretending he needed to settle a debate.
"How can anyone talk or think about such trivial things?" thought Pierre.
"Yes, from Olmütz," he answered with a sigh.

After supper, Pierre and his partner followed the others into the drawing room. The guests began leaving, some without saying goodbye to Hélène. Others came up to her briefly, as if unwilling to distract her from something important, and hurried away, not letting her see them out. The diplomat left the drawing room in mournful silence, reflecting on the pointlessness of his diplomatic career compared to Pierre's happiness. The old general grumbled at his wife when she asked about his leg. 'What an old fool,' he thought. 'That Princess Hélène will still be beautiful at fifty.'
"I believe congratulations are in order," Anna Pavlovna whispered to the old princess, kissing her warmly. "If I didn't have this headache, I would have stayed longer."
The old princess didn't reply. She was tormented by jealousy of her daughter's happiness.

While the guests were leaving, Pierre remained alone with Hélène for a long time in the small drawing room where they had been sitting. He had often been alone with her during the past six weeks but had never spoken of love. Now he felt it was inevitable, yet he couldn't bring himself to take the final step. He felt ashamed; he felt he was occupying someone else's place beside Hélène. 'This happiness is not for you,' some inner voice whispered. 'This happiness is for those who don't have what you have inside you.'
But since he had to say something, he asked if she had enjoyed the party. She replied in her usual simple way that it had been one of the most pleasant name days she could remember.

Some close relatives hadn't left yet and were sitting in the large drawing room. Prince Vasili approached Pierre with slow steps. Pierre stood up and said it was getting late. Prince Vasili gave him a look of stern puzzlement, as if what Pierre had said was too strange to process. But then the severity melted away, and he pulled Pierre's hand down, made him sit, and smiled warmly.

"Well, Lelya?" he said, turning instantly to his daughter with the casual tenderness that parents naturally show children they've spoiled since birth—though Prince Vasili had only learned this manner by imitating other parents.
And he turned back to Pierre.
"Sergei Kuzmich—From all sides—" he said, unbuttoning the top button of his waistcoat.

Pierre smiled, but his smile showed he knew it wasn't the story about Sergei Kuzmich that Prince Vasili was really interested in, and Prince Vasili saw that Pierre knew this. He suddenly mumbled something and walked away. It seemed to Pierre that even the prince was flustered. The sight of this worldly old man's discomfort moved Pierre. He looked at Hélène, and she too seemed flustered, her expression seeming to say: 'Well, it's your own fault.'

"The step has to be taken, but I can't, I can't!" thought Pierre, and he started talking about unimportant things again, about Sergei Kuzmich, asking what the point of the story was, since he hadn't heard it properly. Hélène smiled and said she had missed it too.
When Prince Vasili returned to the drawing room, his wife, the princess, was whispering to the elderly lady about Pierre.
"Of course it's a brilliant match, but happiness, my dear..."
"Marriages are made in heaven," the elderly lady replied.
Prince Vasili walked past, pretending not to hear them, and sat down on a sofa in a far corner. He closed his eyes as if dozing. His head drooped forward, then he roused himself.
"Aline," he said to his wife, "go see what they're doing."
The princess went to the door, walked past it with a dignified, indifferent air, and peeked into the small drawing room. Pierre and Hélène were still sitting and talking, just as before.
"Still the same," she told her husband.

Prince Vasili frowned, his mouth twisting, his cheeks twitching, and his face taking on the coarse, unpleasant expression that was characteristic of him. He shook himself, stood up, threw back his head, and strode purposefully past the ladies into the small drawing room. He walked up to Pierre with quick, joyful steps. His face was so unusually triumphant that Pierre rose in alarm.

"Thank God!" said Prince Vasili. "My wife has told me everything!" He put one arm around Pierre and the other around his daughter. "My dear boy... Lelya... I am so pleased." His voice trembled. "I loved your father... and she will make you a good wife... God bless you!"
He embraced his daughter, then Pierre again, and kissed him. Tears actually wet his cheeks.
"Princess, come here!" he called out.

The old princess came in and wept too. The elderly lady dabbed at her eyes with a handkerchief. Pierre was kissed, and he kissed the beautiful Hélène's hand several times. After a while they were left alone again.

"All this had to happen and couldn't have been otherwise," thought Pierre, "so there's no point asking whether it's good or bad. It's good because it's definite, and I'm free of the old tormenting doubt." Pierre held his fiancée's hand in silence, watching her beautiful chest rise and fall.
"Hélène!" he said aloud, and paused.
"You're supposed to say something special at a moment like this," he thought, but couldn't remember what people say. He looked at her face. She moved closer. Her face flushed.
"Oh, take those off... those..." she said, pointing at his glasses.

Pierre took them off, and his eyes—besides the strange look that eyes always have right after glasses are removed—also had a frightened, questioning expression. He was about to lean over and kiss her hand, but with a quick, almost rough movement, she intercepted his lips with her own. Her face, with its altered, unpleasantly excited expression, startled Pierre.
"It's too late now, it's done. Besides, I love her," thought Pierre.
"I love you!" he said, remembering what you're supposed to say at such moments. But his words sounded so feeble that he felt embarrassed.
"I love you."
Six weeks later he was married and settled in Count Bezukhov's large, newly furnished Petersburg house—the happy owner, as everyone said, of a beautiful, celebrated wife and millions of rubles.

title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 6
paragraphs: It had been a long time since the Rostovs had any news from Nicholas. It wasn't until the middle of winter that the count was finally handed a letter in his son's handwriting. He grabbed it and hurried to his study on tiptoe, anxious and excited, trying not to be noticed. He shut the door and began to read.

Anna Mikhaylovna, who always knew everything that went on in the house, heard about the letter's arrival and quietly slipped into the room. She found the count holding the letter, sobbing and laughing at the same time.
Anna Mikhaylovna's circumstances had improved, but she was still living with the Rostovs.
"My dear friend?" she said in a tone of sympathetic concern, ready to respond to whatever emotion was called for.
The count sobbed even harder.
"Nikolenka... a letter... he w-was... wounded... my dear boy... the countess... promoted to officer... thank God... How do I tell the countess!"

Anna Mikhaylovna sat down beside him, wiped the tears from his eyes and from the letter with her own handkerchief, then dried her own eyes, comforted the count, and came up with a plan: at dinner and through teatime she would prepare the countess, and after tea, with God's help, she would break the news.

At dinner, Anna Mikhaylovna talked constantly about war news and about Nikolenka, twice asking when the last letter from him had arrived — though she already knew. She kept hinting that they might very well receive a letter from him that day. Each time these hints made the countess anxious — she would glance uneasily at the count and at Anna Mikhaylovna — Anna Mikhaylovna deftly steered the conversation to some trivial topic. Natasha, who had the sharpest instincts of anyone in the family for detecting shifts in tone, expression, and mood, had been alert since the start of the meal. She was certain there was some secret between her father and Anna Mikhaylovna, that it had something to do with her brother, and that Anna Mikhaylovna was laying the groundwork. Bold as she was, Natasha knew how sensitive her mother was about anything involving Nikolenka and didn't dare ask questions at the table. But she was too excited to eat and kept squirming in her chair, ignoring her governess's reprimands. After dinner she rushed after Anna Mikhaylovna and, catching up in the sitting room, threw herself on her neck.
"Auntie, darling, please tell me what it is!"
"It's nothing, my dear."
"No, dearest, sweetest, honey — I won't give up. I know you know something."
Anna Mikhaylovna shook her head.
"You little sneak," she said.
"A letter from Nikolenka! I'm sure of it!" Natasha exclaimed, reading the confirmation in Anna Mikhaylovna's face.
"But for God's sake, be careful — you know how it could affect your mother."
"I will, I will, just tell me! You won't? Then I'll go tell everyone right now."
Anna Mikhaylovna gave her a brief summary of the letter's contents, on the condition that she tell no one.
"No, I swear on my honor," said Natasha, crossing herself, "I won't tell anyone!" And she immediately ran off to find Sonya.
"Nikolenka... wounded... a letter," she announced in gleeful triumph.
"Nicholas!" was all Sonya managed, instantly turning white.
Seeing the impact the news of her brother's wound had on Sonya, Natasha felt for the first time the painful side of it.
She threw her arms around Sonya and began to cry.
"It's just a small wound, but he's been made an officer. He's fine now — he wrote the letter himself," she said through her tears.

"There, you see! All you women are such crybabies," said Petya, striding around the room with large, determined steps. "I'm very glad, very glad indeed, that my brother has distinguished himself. You're all blubberers who don't understand anything."
Natasha smiled through her tears.
"Have you read the letter?" Sonya asked.
"No, but she said it's all over and that he's an officer now."
"Thank God!" said Sonya, crossing herself. "But maybe she wasn't telling the truth. Let's go to Mama."
Petya paced the room in silence for a moment.
"If I'd been in Nikolenka's place, I would have killed even more of those Frenchmen," he said. "What awful brutes they are! I would have killed so many there'd have been a pile of them."
"Be quiet, Petya — you're being ridiculous!"
"I'm not ridiculous — it's the people who cry over nothing who are ridiculous," Petya retorted.
"Do you remember him?" Natasha asked suddenly, after a moment of silence.
Sonya smiled.
"Do I remember Nicholas?"

"No, Sonya, what I mean is — do you remember him so well that you can picture him perfectly, everything about him?" Natasha said with an emphatic gesture, clearly trying to give her words a very specific meaning. "I remember Nikolenka too — I remember him well. But I don't remember Boris. Not at all."
"What! You don't remember Boris?" Sonya asked in surprise.

"It's not that I don't remember — I know what he looks like, but not the way I remember Nikolenka. With him, I just close my eyes and he's there. But Boris..." She shut her eyes. "No! Nothing at all."

"Oh, Natasha!" said Sonya, gazing at her friend with an intensity and seriousness that suggested she was saying something too important for jokes, almost as if speaking to someone else entirely. "I am in love with your brother, once and for all, and whatever may happen to him or to me, I will never stop loving him as long as I live."

Natasha looked at Sonya with curious, wondering eyes and said nothing. She felt that Sonya was telling the truth, that such love existed. But Natasha had never felt anything like it herself. She believed it was possible, but she didn't understand it.
"Will you write to him?" she asked.

Sonya grew thoughtful. The question of how to write to Nicholas, and whether she even should, tormented her. Now that he was an officer and a wounded hero, would it be right to remind him of her existence and of the promises he'd made?
"I don't know. I think if he writes to me, I'll write back," she said, blushing.
"And you wouldn't feel embarrassed writing to him?"
Sonya smiled.
"No."
"Well, I'd be embarrassed to write to Boris. I'm not going to."
"Why would you be embarrassed?"
"I don't know. It's just awkward. It would make me feel strange."

"I know why she'd be embarrassed," said Petya, still stinging from Natasha's earlier remark. "It's because she was in love with that fat one in glasses" — that was how Petya described his namesake, the new Count Bezukhov — "and now she's in love with that singer" — meaning Natasha's Italian singing teacher. "That's why she's embarrassed!"
"Petya, you're an idiot!" said Natasha.
"No more of an idiot than you, madam," said the nine-year-old Petya, with the air of a seasoned brigadier.

The countess had been prepared by Anna Mikhaylovna's hints at dinner. After retiring to her room, she sat in an armchair with her eyes fixed on a miniature portrait of her son on the lid of a snuffbox, tears steadily filling her eyes. Anna Mikhaylovna came tiptoeing to the countess's door with the letter and paused.
"Don't come in," she said to the old count, who was following her. "Come later." She went in and closed the door behind her.
The count pressed his ear to the keyhole and listened.

At first he heard the murmur of ordinary conversation, then Anna Mikhaylovna's voice alone in a long speech, then a cry, then silence, then both voices together in happy tones, and finally footsteps. Anna Mikhaylovna opened the door. Her face wore the proud expression of a surgeon who has just performed a difficult operation and is now allowing the audience to admire his skill.

"It's done!" she said to the count, gesturing triumphantly toward the countess, who sat holding the snuffbox with the portrait in one hand and the letter in the other, pressing them alternately to her lips.

When the countess saw the count, she stretched her arms out to him, embraced his bald head, and — looking past it at the letter and portrait — gently pushed it aside so she could press them to her lips once more. Vera, Natasha, Sonya, and Petya came into the room, and the reading of the letter began. After a brief description of the campaign and the two battles he'd fought in, along with his promotion, Nicholas wrote that he kissed his father's and mother's hands and asked for their blessing. He sent his love to Vera, Natasha, and Petya. He also sent greetings to Monsieur Schelling, Madame Schoss, and his old nanny, and asked them to kiss "dear Sonya, whom he loved and thought of just as always." When Sonya heard this, she blushed so deeply that tears sprang to her eyes and, unable to bear everyone's stares, she ran into the ballroom, spun around at full speed with her skirt billowing out like a balloon, and then, flushed and smiling, collapsed onto the floor. The countess was crying.
"Why are you crying, Mama?" Vera asked. "From everything he says, we should be happy, not crying."
This was perfectly true, but the count, the countess, and Natasha all looked at her reproachfully. "Who does she take after?" the countess thought.

Nicholas's letter was read hundreds of times, and anyone deemed worthy of hearing it had to come to the countess — she wouldn't let it out of her hands. The tutors came, and the nannies, and Dmitri, and several acquaintances, and each time the countess reread the letter with renewed pleasure, discovering fresh evidence of Nikolenka's virtues. How strange, how extraordinary, how wonderful it seemed that her son — the boy whose tiny movements she had felt inside her twenty years ago, the son she used to argue about with the overly indulgent count, the son who had first learned to say "pear" and then "granny" — that this son was now far away in a foreign land among strangers, a real man doing a man's work on his own, without help or guidance. The universal human experience, showing that children grow up gradually from cradle to adulthood, simply didn't exist for the countess. Every stage of her son's development had seemed just as miraculous to her as if no other child in history had ever grown up the same way. Just as it had once seemed impossible that the tiny creature living beneath her heart would ever cry, nurse at her breast, and learn to speak, so now she couldn't believe that little creature had become this strong, brave man, this model son and officer that his letter revealed him to be.

"What a style! How beautifully he describes things!" she said, reading the descriptive passages. "And what a soul! Not a word about himself... not a word! Something about some Denisov or other, though I'm sure he himself is braver than all of them. He says nothing about his own suffering. What a heart! How typical of him! And he remembered everyone! Didn't forget a single person. I always said, even when he was only this tall — I always said..."

For more than a week, preparations went on: drafts of letters to Nicholas from every member of the household were written and recopied, and under the countess's supervision and the count's careful attention, money and everything needed for the newly commissioned officer's uniform and equipment were gathered together. Anna Mikhaylovna, practical woman that she was, had even used her connections in the military to arrange an efficient way to send mail for herself and her son. She had access to a courier service going to Grand Duke Constantine Pavlovich, who commanded the Guards. The Rostovs assumed that "The Russian Guards, Abroad" was a perfectly adequate address, and that if a letter reached the Grand Duke commanding the Guards, there was no reason it couldn't be forwarded to the Pavlograd regiment, which was presumably somewhere nearby. So they decided to send the letters and money via the Grand Duke's courier to Boris, who would forward them to Nicholas. The letters came from the old count, the countess, Petya, Vera, Natasha, and Sonya, along with six thousand rubles for his outfitting and various other things the count sent his son.
